GENERAL.label: Overall views, background and definitions
GENERAL.covers: Views on FDA's approach or on generative AI in healthcare as a whole (general support, hopes, worries or opposition), proposals that span several parts of the paper, such as a whole-lifecycle framework, and points about the paper's framing: its introduction, background, definitions of terms such as generative AI or foundation model, and which products count as devices (Sections I-III and VIII, which ask no numbered questions).
GENERAL.cues: support FDA's approach, too risky, promising, general worries about errors or hallucinations, definitions, scope
GENERAL.excludes: A specific proposal about one part of the paper goes to that part's code, even when it opens with a general remark. A worry about something the paper doesn't address, such as privacy or cost, even when stated as a general concern, is not tagged: it is skipped as outside the paper.

RISK.label: Assessing a device's risk
RISK.covers: How FDA should judge how risky a device is (Section IV, Questions 1-6). FDA proposes two axes: how independently the device acts, from giving neutral information, to directing what someone should do, to taking actions such as prescribing on its own; and how severe the harm would be if someone relied on a wrong output. Also covered: patient-facing versus clinician-facing use, generalist versus specialist users, risks that build up over a multi-turn conversation, and failing to escalate care or escalating it needlessly.
RISK.cues: risk framework, risk tiers, autonomy, severity of harm, patient-facing, escalation, triage, human in the loop
RISK.excludes: General warnings that AI is dangerous (GENERAL). How much evidence a device needs given its risk (PREMARKET). Systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks with tools (AGENTIC).

PREMARKET.label: Evaluating a device before it is sold
PREMARKET.covers: What a device should demonstrate before FDA authorizes it (Section V, Questions 7-17). FDA proposes a competency-based approach with two parts: benchmarking, meaning large-scale testing of the finished device's knowledge, reasoning, safety behavior and communication across many inputs; and clinical confirmation, meaning evidence that it performs as intended in real or realistic clinical use. Also covered: scaling evidence to the device's risk, statistics, synthetic test data, comparators and acceptance criteria for open-ended outputs, comparison with care without the device, independent third-party testing, and other model architectures.
PREMARKET.cues: benchmark, validation, test set, red-teaming, clinical study, performance metrics, acceptance threshold, synthetic data, independent lab, before clearance
PREMARKET.excludes: Re-testing after the device is on the market, for example after an update (POSTMARKET). Testing specific to agentic systems (AGENTIC).

POSTMARKET.label: Oversight once a device is in use
POSTMARKET.covers: How devices are watched and changed after they reach the market (Section VI, Questions 18-24). Monitoring: tracking real-world performance, drift and errors, audit trails, whether AI supervisory agents could do some of the monitoring, and accepting more uncertainty before sale in return for stronger monitoring after. Shared responsibility: the roles of manufacturers, clinicians, hospitals, payers and others in monitoring and reporting. Changes: software updates, retraining, models that keep learning, how much evidence each change needs, predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), and changes made by a third-party foundation model's developer.
POSTMARKET.cues: postmarket, real-world performance, drift, monitoring, audit, adverse event reporting, update, retraining, version, PCCP, change control
POSTMARKET.excludes: A clinician monitoring a patient, which is care, not device oversight. The voluntary master file program (MASTER_FILES).

MASTER_FILES.label: Foundation model master files
MASTER_FILES.covers: FDA's idea of voluntary Foundation Model Master Files (Section VII.A, Question 25): the developer of a foundation model would confidentially give FDA information about it, such as a model card, known limitations, evaluation results and update commitments, which device makers could reference, with the developer's permission, in their own submissions.
MASTER_FILES.cues: master file, MAF, model card, system card, foundation model developer, confidential
MASTER_FILES.excludes: How a device maker should handle a third-party model's updates after launch (POSTMARKET).

AGENTIC.label: Agentic AI systems
AGENTIC.covers: Agentic AI (Section VII.B, Question 26): systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, use external tools, or take a sequence of actions, for example in care coordination, documentation, patient outreach or workflow support; and how FDA should approach them, including which of these functions should count as devices.
AGENTIC.cues: agent, agentic, autonomous workflow, multi-step, tool use, orchestration
AGENTIC.excludes: The risk of a device taking a single action, such as prescribing (RISK). AI supervisory agents that monitor a device in use (POSTMARKET).

skip.label: Skipped: no point about the paper
skip.covers: Text that makes no point about the paper: greetings, thanks, introductions of the writer, disclaimers, signatures, contact details, and lead-ins that only announce a list of points to come. Also a substantive point about a topic the paper does not address, when it is not tied to any part of FDA's proposal: privacy and data protection, security of networks and stored data, legal liability, reimbursement and cost, labeling, workforce and staff training, adoption in practice, interoperability, intellectual property, or an ethical concern. For such a point, the reason names the topic.
skip.cues: thank you, sincerely, on behalf of, in my individual capacity, the following points
skip.excludes: Thanks or an introduction that also states a view, such as support for FDA's direction, gets a tag for that view (GENERAL). A heading that introduces a paragraph is not skipped: it is tagged together with that paragraph, as a range. A point on one of those topics that concerns a part of FDA's proposal is tagged with that part's code: data sensitivity as a factor in a device's risk (RISK); attacks through a device's inputs, such as prompt injection, and automation bias, when they concern testing before sale (PREMARKET); privacy safeguards in monitoring, and who is accountable for deploying and monitoring a device (POSTMARKET); what foundation model developers disclose or protect through master files (MASTER_FILES); FDA's own legal authority, and overall views on generative AI in healthcare (GENERAL).

support.label: Supports FDA's approach
support.covers: Agrees with what FDA proposed on this point, as it stands.
support.cues: we support, agree, welcome, appropriately recognizes
support.excludes: Agreement that comes with a request for a small change (conditional-minor) or a larger one (conditional-major).

conditional-minor.label: Supports it with small changes
conditional-minor.covers: Accepts FDA's approach on this point and asks for a small change: one after which the approach would still work the same way. The approach may be spelled out (a clarification, a definition, an example, more detail), extended with more of the same (further tests, further factors to weigh), or given different settings (where it applies, how much, how often). Use it also when it is unclear whether the approach would work differently.
conditional-minor.excludes: A change to how the approach works (conditional-major). Narrowing the approach until almost nothing is left of it (oppose). Agreement that asks for nothing (support). The size of the change decides, not how firmly it is asked for.

conditional-major.label: Supports it with larger changes
conditional-major.covers: Accepts FDA's direction on this point but asks for a larger change: one after which the approach would work differently. A core element is added, replaced or removed, or a defining feature is reversed: for example a third axis in a two-axis framework, a different comparator, a pass-or-fail limit that an average cannot offset, or a voluntary program made mandatory. A point that asks for both a small and a larger change belongs here.
conditional-major.excludes: A change that leaves the approach working the same way, such as where it applies or how much detail it gives (conditional-minor). Rejecting the approach itself (oppose). Information that takes no position (neutral). The size of the change decides, not how firmly it is asked for.

oppose.label: Opposes FDA's approach
oppose.covers: Disagrees with what FDA proposed on this point, or argues against the direction as a whole.
oppose.cues: should not, oppose, too risky, unnecessary, instead of
oppose.excludes: Accepting the approach while asking for a small change (conditional-minor) or a larger one (conditional-major).

neutral.label: Takes no position
neutral.covers: Information, examples or concerns that take no position on what FDA proposed.
neutral.cues: for example, in our experience, I want to note
neutral.excludes: A concern offered as a reason for a small change to FDA's approach (conditional-minor), a larger one (conditional-major) or its rejection (oppose).

GEN.label: Overall approach and general views
GEN.covers: Views on the paper or FDA's direction as a whole rather than on one question: overall support, concerns or opposition; regulatory philosophy (risk-based oversight, least burdensome principles, total product life cycle, balancing innovation with safety); whether, when and how FDA should move to guidance, rules, pilots or further engagement; legal-authority questions; consistency with existing FDA AI policies; international harmonization; comment-process requests such as extensions or public meetings.
GEN.cues: total product life cycle, TPLC, harmonization

BKG.label: GenAI characteristics, risks and benefits
BKG.covers: General discussion of what makes GenAI-enabled devices different (Section II) when not tied to a specific proposal: benefits such as personalization, adaptability and access, and characteristic risks such as confabulation or hallucination, output variability, unclear bounds of intended use, opacity of third-party foundation models and performance degradation, including evidence or real-world examples of these.

DEF.label: Definitions, scope and device status
DEF.covers: Section III: definitions of GenAI, foundation model, large language model, agentic AI system and multimodal; what counts as a GenAI-enabled device or device software function; which GenAI functions are devices, fall outside the device definition, are excluded under section 520(o) (including the clinical decision support criteria) or sit under enforcement discretion; multiple-function products and 'other functions'; the principle that FDA regulates devices rather than GenAI itself; requests to clarify the regulatory status of particular product types such as ambient scribes, documentation, administrative or wellness tools.

Q1.label: Two-axis risk framework and additional dimensions
Q1.covers: Whether a risk framework built on two axes (how much the function acts or directs action, and how severe the harm is from relying on a wrong output) captures what matters for GenAI risk; whether and how to add dimensions such as reversibility of the resulting action, downstream safeguards, time pressure in the setting, or traceability of outputs to primary sources. Also the parts of Section IV that ask no numbered question: FDA's view that functions that take clinical action (assigning a diagnosis, prescribing, initiating an order set) are typically higher risk than informational ones, moderated by the severity of consequences and the level of clinician supervision, with views on autonomy levels and supervision in risk assessment; and FDA's view that in vitro diagnostic, measurement and signal-processing functions may be higher risk even though non-directive, because users usually cannot check the output independently.

Q2.label: Directiveness spectrum for informational functions
Q2.covers: How to handle informational functions that range from non-directive to action-directing; which output features (wording, specificity, personalization, context) should raise or lower risk once intended use is accounted for; what would give manufacturers clarity and predictability given that directiveness is a continuum. Includes FDA's views that substance and context matter more than trigger words, that disclaimers such as 'talk to your doctor' may not make an output less directive, and that consequence severity moderates the risk of action-directing outputs.

Q3.label: Patient-facing vs clinician-facing functions
Q3.covers: Whether and when delivering clinical information to patients rather than clinicians creates different or higher risk, weighed against empowerment, engagement, access and avoiding paternalism; which device characteristics, output features or safeguards reduce risk for users who cannot evaluate outputs, without underestimating patients.

Q4.label: Generalist vs specialist clinician users
Q4.covers: Whether the generalist/specialist distinction should shape risk for clinician-facing functions; when risk changes if a clinician without the relevant specialty training receives specialist-domain output; characteristics and safeguards that mitigate this; the potential to extend access to specialty knowledge.

Q5.label: Multi-turn conversational risk
Q5.covers: How to assess risk across realistic conversation trajectories when a conversational device can drift from non-directive to action-directing output; how to describe intended use when behavior emerges over a conversation.

Q6.label: Care escalation: under- vs over-escalation
Q6.covers: How to characterize and weigh under-escalation (failing to send someone to needed care) against over-escalation (unneeded emergency care, anxiety, cost, eroded trust), given that the two errors are not directly comparable and acceptable trade-offs differ by clinical context.

Q7.label: Competency-based approach overall
Q7.covers: Whether device benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation is a useful and appropriate premarket framework; evaluating the final, configured, user-facing device rather than the foundation model alone; the analogy to how clinicians are trained, examined, licensed and credentialed, and critiques of it such as accountability gaps; tailoring the approach to intended use and risk in general.

Q8.label: Using the risk framework to scale premarket evidence
Q8.covers: How the two-axis risk framework could set the level of premarket evidence: which benchmarking elements apply, the range and difficulty of test conditions, and how much clinical confirmation is needed.

Q9.label: Benchmarking structure and methods
Q9.covers: Whether the proposed benchmarking elements (safety, clinical proficiency, generalizability, agentic) would give adequate evidence of safety and effectiveness; missing, redundant or miscategorized elements; external standards that could be used. Also the general benchmarking principles: prespecified methods and acceptance criteria, scoring rubrics grounded in guidelines or expert input, independent adjudicators (including LLM adjudicators), enough clinical scope, datasets representative of deployment settings, and simulation, synthetic test generation or virtual patients. It also covers points about any single benchmarking element: safety-critical recognition and escalation; scope maintenance and boundary adherence; calibration, uncertainty and clinical deferral; clinical knowledge and task fidelity; information gathering and clinical analysis; quantitative and measurement analysis; communication quality and user comprehension; robustness, reliability and reproducibility; subgroup performance. Testing specific to agentic systems goes to AGENTIC (Q26).

Q10.label: Benchmark validity and sponsor-developed benchmarks
Q10.covers: How a sponsor can show that benchmark performance predicts safe and effective real-world behavior; what evidence supports a benchmark's construct validity; what role sponsor-built benchmarks should play given independence and teaching-to-the-test concerns; how contamination, saturation and limited representativeness of public benchmarks affect the approach.
Q10.cues: data contamination, construct validity, public benchmarks

Q11.label: Choosing a clinical confirmation approach
Q11.covers: How a sponsor should select and justify a clinical confirmation approach proportionate to intended use and risk, given FDA's view that a prospective study may not always be needed; the options (retrospective evaluation on real inputs, shadow deployment, standardized patient interactions, clinician adjudication of real cases, blinded or unblinded, and prospective studies or randomized trials); device types or risk profiles for which options fall short; accounting for the real-world input distribution; other confirmation methods.

V-RWD.label: Real-world and ex-US data in clinical confirmation (no numbered question)
V-RWD.covers: Considerations for using real-world data and data collected outside the United States in clinical confirmation, which FDA invited in the text of Section V.C.

Q12.label: Statistical rigor and combining evidence
Q12.covers: How to get statistically meaningful performance estimates; accounting for differences between synthetic and real-world input distributions; when benchmarking and clinical confirmation evidence may be combined into one estimate; how endpoints and sample sizes should be set when studies are not powered for traditional effectiveness endpoints.

Q13.label: Suitability and safeguards for synthetic data
Q13.covers: Which clinical domains, device functions or subpopulations synthetic data suits well or poorly as a supplement to real-world evidence; safeguards against synthetic data generated by the same class of model reproducing the gaps the evaluation should catch, especially for underrepresented subgroups; use of synthetic data for small or hard-to-sample subgroups.

Q14.label: Comparators and acceptance criteria for open-ended outputs
Q14.covers: How to choose comparators and acceptance criteria when many different outputs can be acceptable; clinician panels and whether the standard should be the standard of care or a median practicing clinician; generalist vs specialist comparators; when to evaluate human-AI team performance rather than the device alone; setting performance thresholds; using a conventional reference standard where one exists.

Q15.label: Comparing with care in the device's absence
Q15.covers: Assessing performance against what would happen without the device (unaided clinical judgment, delayed specialist review, no intervention) instead of expert comparators; how to identify and justify such comparators.
Q15.cues: absence of the device, no intervention, delayed specialist review

Q16.label: Role of independent third parties
Q16.covers: Whether and how qualified, independent third parties should take part in benchmarking and clinical confirmation (conducting or evaluating assessments and issuing certificates, maintaining sequestered datasets, adjudicating, building FDA-qualified tools, developing recognized standards); qualification and independence criteria; where third-party involvement is impractical; safeguards so it does not limit competition or innovation; analogies to FDA's ASCA and MDDT programs.
Q16.cues: accreditation, ASCA, sequestered datasets, competition, bottleneck

Q17.label: Other model architectures
Q17.covers: Whether the competency-based approach works for other architectures such as multimodal vision-language models and generative or predictive world models; what would be ineffective or inapplicable; what additional considerations apply.

Q18.label: Trading premarket uncertainty for postmarket monitoring
Q18.covers: Conditions under which FDA could accept more uncertainty about benefit-risk at market entry by relying more on postmarket monitoring; what a monitoring program would need to justify less premarket evidence; device types or risk profiles for which this would be inappropriate.

Q19.label: Postmarket performance evaluation approaches
Q19.covers: Periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review and performance degradation (drift) monitoring: feasibility, additional approaches, and how to set the cadence and triggering events for reassessment.
Q19.cues: performance degradation, adverse event reporting, MDR

Q20.label: Machine-based supervisory agents
Q20.covers: Whether postmarket monitoring can be supported by machine-based supervisory agents, and what to consider, including how the supervisory agent itself is evaluated and how reliable it is.

Q21.label: Shared ecosystem roles and accountability
Q21.covers: Roles for clinicians, health systems, professional societies, standards bodies, payers, public-private consortia and other authorities in deploying, monitoring and reporting on GenAI-enabled devices; how to structure those roles without diluting the manufacturer's accountability.
Q21.cues: local validation, shared responsibility, manufacturer accountability

Q22.label: Scaling evidence for modifications; what a PCCP can cover
Q22.covers: Using the premarket competency assessment as a baseline for re-evaluating changes; scaling re-benchmarking or other evidence to a change's nature and expected impact; which changes could be handled within the quality system and which need FDA review before implementation; which change categories suit a PCCP (for example prompt, retrieval, guardrail, orchestration, interface or model updates).
Q22.cues: quality management system, guardrail changes, change categories

Q23.label: Adapting PCCPs to changes that can't be fully prespecified
Q23.covers: How PCCP concepts or other change-control approaches could work when the nature or scope of future modifications cannot be fully specified in advance, including model-evolution changes from continuous or adaptive learning.

Q24.label: Changes initiated by third-party foundation model developers
Q24.covers: How manufacturers can detect, evaluate and respond in time to changes made by the developer of an underlying third-party foundation model; contractual, technical or PCCP mechanisms that provide assurance, for example version pinning, advance notice, deprecation schedules, regression testing and supplier controls.

Q25.label: Voluntary Foundation Model Master Files
Q25.covers: Whether voluntary Foundation Model Master Files under the Device Master File program are practical for developers to provide and keep current; what they should contain (model or system cards, architecture, training data provenance, supported uses, limitations and failure modes, healthcare benchmark results including subgroups, guardrails, update-notification commitments, audit logs); how to make a voluntary program useful given weak incentives to disclose; alternative ways to get information about foundation models.
Q25.cues: master file, MAF, model card, training data provenance, alternative mechanisms

Q26.label: Agentic AI systems
Q26.covers: Additional premarket and postmarket considerations for agentic GenAI-enabled devices; reflecting the higher risk of autonomous multi-step action, tool use and reduced human review in acceptance criteria and oversight; device status of agentic uses such as care coordination, documentation, outreach or control of other devices.
